title: OCaml
subtitle: A fast, statically typed functional language with a powerful module system and, since OCaml 5, multicore parallelism and effect handlers, from a first program to professional practice.
description: OCaml is a general-purpose programming language from the ML family, developed at Inria in France and first released as Objective Caml in 1996. It combines functional programming (immutable data, pattern matching, higher-order functions) with practical imperative features (mutable references, arrays, exceptions), a type system that infers almost every type without annotations, and a module system that is among the most expressive of any language. It compiles to fast native code with a predictable garbage collector. OCaml is used to write compilers and static analysers, proof assistants such as Rocq (formerly Coq), trading systems at Jane Street, the Tezos blockchain, MirageOS unikernels and many developer tools.

This course is for anyone who already knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. No previous functional programming is assumed. It starts with installing OCaml and running a first program, works through expressions, functions, lists, options, records and variants, then modules, signatures and functors, mutability and exceptions, and the standard library, and ends with OCaml 5's domains and effect handlers, the tools OCaml teams use every day, and a complete small project.

To run the code, install OCaml with opam, its package manager, following the instructions at [ocaml.org/install](https://ocaml.org/install); you can also try programs in the browser at the [OCaml Playground](https://ocaml.org/play). Every complete program in these lessons was run with OCaml 5.4 by Lumenary's test suite, and the output shown is the output it printed. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: Install OCaml with opam, run programs in the toplevel and with dune, and learn the core language: expressions and inferred types, functions, lists, options, results, records and variants, all taken apart with pattern matching.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: Organise code with modules, signatures and functors, use mutable state, arrays and exceptions where they help, and do everyday work with the standard library.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: Use OCaml 5's domains for parallelism and effect handlers for concurrency, work with the tools OCaml teams rely on, see honestly where OCaml is used, and build a complete project.
